ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: In the image, A of triangle ABC is above, B is at the lower left, C is at the lower right, point D is located on side AC, and segment BD is drawn; there is no obvious right-angle mark in the figure, but the problem statement clearly gives that BD is perpendicular to AC. Let AD=m and CD=n, then AC=m+n. Because AB=AC, AB=m+n. Since D is on AC and BD⊥AC, triangle ABD is a right triangle, with the right angle at D. By the Pythagorean theorem, AB^2=AD^2+BD^2, that is, (m+n)^2=m^2+57. Rearranging gives (m+n)^2-m^2=57, so n(2m+n)=57. Because m,n are positive integers, the positive factor decompositions of 57 are 1×57 and 3×19. If n=1 and 2m+n=57, then 2m=56, m=28, AC=m+n=29. If n=3 and 2m+n=19, then 2m=16, m=8, AC=m+n=11. Therefore the smallest possible AC is 11.

method.method_draft: Let AD=m and CD=n, so AC=m+n. From the text, AB=AC, so AB=m+n. From the image/text, BD is perpendicular to AC at D, making triangle ABD right. Apply the Pythagorean theorem in right triangle ABD: AB^2=AD^2+BD^2, so (m+n)^2=m^2+57. Rearrange to n(2m+n)=57, or equivalently ((m+n)-m)((m+n)+m)=57. Since m,n are positive integers, factor 57: the possible factor pairs are (1,57) and (3,19). These give AC=(1+57)/2=29 or AC=(3+19)/2=11. The smallest possible AC is 11.
